question: What is @Entity in JPA and what does it do?
title: @Entity Annotation in JPA Explained
direct_answer: **`@Entity`** marks a Java class as a JPA-managed entity that maps to a database table. JPA scans for `@Entity` classes at startup and creates a table mapping for each. The class must have a no-arg constructor and a field annotated with `@Id` for the primary key.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the requirements: @Id, no-arg constructor, and non-final class

sections.title: Basic @Entity Class
@Entity Requirements
sections.content:
- **`@Id`**: required — marks the primary key field
- **No-arg constructor**: required — JPA uses it to create instances
- **Non-final class**: required — Hibernate uses subclassing for proxies
- `@Table(name="...")`: optional — defaults to class name
- `@Column(name="...")`: optional — defaults to field name
- Class must be in a scanned package (Spring Boot: under main class package)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Entity` tells JPA that this Java class should be mapped to a database table. By default, the table name matches the class name. There are three requirements for an entity class: it must have `@Id` on one field for the primary key, it must have a no-arg constructor so JPA can create instances when loading from the database, and it shouldn't be final because Hibernate creates subclass proxies for lazy loading. You can customize the mapping with `@Table` for the table name and `@Column` for individual column settings like name, nullable, and length.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Entity is the starting point of every JPA mapping — without it, Hibernate doesn't know the class exists.

beats.heading: What it does
beats.body: @Entity marks a Java class as a database-mapped entity. JPA scans for @Entity classes at startup and builds a mapping between each class and a database table. By default, the table name matches the class name — a User class maps to a user table.

beats.heading: Three requirements
items: @Id on one field — JPA needs to know which field is the primary key.
A no-arg constructor — JPA uses it to create instances when loading rows from the database.
The class must not be final — Hibernate creates proxy subclasses for lazy loading, which requires subclassing.

beats.heading: Optional customization
beats.body: Use @Table(name="tbl_users") when your table name differs from the class name. Use @Column(name="first_name") when your column name differs from the field name. Both are optional — if you skip them, JPA uses the class and field names as-is.

beats.heading: Candidates miss
beats.body: candidates miss: forgetting the no-arg constructor when they add a custom constructor. If you define any constructor with parameters, Java no longer provides a default no-arg constructor. You have to add it back explicitly, or JPA will throw an exception when loading entities from the database.

sections.cap: @Entity marks the class, @Id marks the key, and a no-arg constructor lets JPA create instances. Those three are non-negotiable.
followup_handoff: They'll often follow up with why the no-arg constructor is required — JPA uses reflection to instantiate entities.
@GeneratedValue strategies are a natural next question after @Id.

followup_questions: Why does JPA require a no-arg constructor?
What is @Table and when do you need it?

question: What is @Id and @GeneratedValue in JPA?
title: @Id and @GeneratedValue in JPA
direct_answer: **`@Id`** marks the primary key field. **`@GeneratedValue`** controls how the ID is generated. The four strategies are: `IDENTITY` (database auto-increment — most common), `SEQUENCE` (database sequence), `TABLE` (JPA-managed table), `AUTO` (JPA picks based on DB).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using GenerationType.AUTO and not understanding what it picks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which strategy to use for MySQL (IDENTITY) vs PostgreSQL (SEQUENCE)

rows: JPA manages a separate sequence table
JPA picks based on DB type

sections.title: @Id and @GeneratedValue
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Id` marks the primary key field — every JPA entity must have one. `@GeneratedValue` tells JPA how to auto-generate the ID value. The most common strategy is `IDENTITY` which uses the database's auto-increment feature — this is what you use with MySQL. `SEQUENCE` uses database sequences, which is the PostgreSQL and Oracle approach and allows better batch performance. `AUTO` lets JPA decide — it works fine for demos but you should explicitly choose the right strategy for production. I'd typically use `IDENTITY` for MySQL projects and `SEQUENCE` for PostgreSQL.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Id marks the primary key. @GeneratedValue tells the database how to fill it in automatically.

beats.heading: What each does
beats.body: @Id marks which field is the primary key — every entity must have exactly one. @GeneratedValue goes on top of it and tells JPA to auto-generate the value rather than require you to set it manually.

beats.heading: The four strategies
values: JPA manages its own sequence table

beats.heading: Which one to pick
beats.body: Use IDENTITY for MySQL — it maps to AUTO_INCREMENT. Use SEQUENCE for PostgreSQL and Oracle — sequences allow Hibernate to batch ID allocation in chunks, which is faster for bulk inserts. Avoid TABLE in production because it uses a lock on a separate table to generate IDs, which becomes a bottleneck.

beats.heading: Sharp edge
beats.body: sharp edge: with IDENTITY strategy, Hibernate can't batch INSERT statements. The database must execute each INSERT and return the generated ID before Hibernate can continue. SEQUENCE avoids this by pre-fetching a range of IDs. If your app does a lot of bulk inserts, SEQUENCE with a high allocationSize is noticeably faster.

sections.cap: Use IDENTITY for MySQL. Use SEQUENCE for PostgreSQL. Avoid AUTO in production — let it pick in demos, but be explicit when it matters.
followup_handoff: They may ask why TABLE strategy is slow — the lock on the sequence table is the answer.
Composite primary keys are a related question — @EmbeddedId and @IdClass are the two JPA approaches.

followup_questions: What is the difference between GenerationType.IDENTITY and SEQUENCE?
Can you have a composite primary key in JPA?

question: What is @Column in JPA and what can you configure with it?
title: @Column Annotation in JPA Configurations
direct_answer: **`@Column`** customizes the database column mapping for a field. Key attributes: `name` (column name), `nullable` (allow NULL?), `length` (VARCHAR length), `unique` (unique constraint), `columnDefinition` (custom DDL type). Without `@Column`, the field name is used as the column name.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not using nullable=false and length constraints — important for DB schema quality
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Column constraints affect DDL generation but not runtime validation

sections.title: @Column Usage
Key @Column Attributes
sections.content:
- `name`: custom column name (default: field name)
- `nullable=false`: NOT NULL constraint in DDL
- `length`: VARCHAR length (default: 255)
- `unique`: UNIQUE constraint
- `precision/scale`: for BigDecimal fields
- `columnDefinition`: raw SQL column type
- `insertable/updatable=false`: exclude from INSERT/UPDATE SQL
- Note: `nullable=false` affects schema generation, NOT bean validation — use `@NotNull` for runtime

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Column` is used to customize how a Java field maps to a database column. The most common attributes are `name` to change the column name — useful when your Java field name doesn't match the DB naming convention — `nullable=false` to add a NOT NULL constraint to the schema, and `length` to control VARCHAR length. One important thing to clarify: `nullable=false` in `@Column` only affects schema generation — it adds NOT NULL to the CREATE TABLE statement. It doesn't validate at the application level. If you want runtime validation to reject null values, you need `@NotNull` from Bean Validation separately.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Column is optional — but skipping it means accepting all the defaults, and those defaults can bite you.

beats.heading: What it does
beats.body: @Column customizes how a Java field maps to a database column. Without it, JPA uses the field name as the column name and VARCHAR(255) as the type for String fields. Use @Column when you need to override any of that.

beats.heading: The attributes you'll use most
items: name — map to a differently named column, like name="first_name" for a firstName field.
nullable=false — adds NOT NULL to the DDL column definition.
length — set VARCHAR length for String fields. Default is 255.
unique — adds a UNIQUE constraint on that single column.
precision and scale — required for BigDecimal to map to DECIMAL(10,2) correctly.

beats.heading: DDL vs runtime validation
beats.body: nullable=false only affects the CREATE TABLE statement when Hibernate generates the schema. It does not validate the value at runtime. If you try to save a null value, the database will reject it — but your application won't catch it until it hits the database. Add @NotNull from Bean Validation if you want the error to surface earlier, at the service layer.

beats.heading: Non-obvious
beats.body: non-obvious: the default VARCHAR(255) for String fields is a silent trap. A field with no @Column(length=...) generates a 255-character column. Try to save a 300-character description and the database truncates or rejects it at runtime. Always set length for String fields that could hold more than 255 characters.

sections.cap: @Column is your control panel for column naming, nullability, length, and uniqueness. The most important habit is always setting nullable=false and length intentionally rather than relying on defaults.
followup_handoff: A common follow-up is the difference between @Column(nullable=false) and @NotNull — they operate at different layers.
They might ask about columnDefinition for mapping to TEXT or other database-specific types.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Column(nullable=false) and @NotNull?
What is the default length for @Column?
How do you map a BigDecimal to a database decimal column?

question: What is @Table in JPA and when do you use it?
title: @Table Annotation in JPA
direct_answer: **`@Table`** specifies the database table name, schema, and catalog for a JPA entity. Without it, the table name defaults to the entity class name. Use `@Table(name="products")` when your table name differs from the class name or follows a different naming convention.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not using @Table when there's a naming mismatch between Java and DB convention
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Table's uniqueConstraints attribute for adding multi-column unique constraints

sections.title: @Table Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- Default table name = class name (case depends on DB)
- `@Table(name="...")` — custom table name
- `schema`: specify database schema (useful for PostgreSQL/Oracle)
- `catalog`: specify database catalog
- `uniqueConstraints`: add multi-column UNIQUE constraints
- `indexes`: add database indexes (for DDL generation)
- Spring Boot naming strategy: `User` → `user` table by default (spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.physical-strategy)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Table` customizes which database table an entity maps to. By default, JPA uses the class name as the table name. If your table has a different name — like `tbl_users` instead of `user`, or the DB uses a different case convention — you need `@Table(name="tbl_users")`. It also lets you specify a schema name, which is useful in PostgreSQL or Oracle environments where tables are organized in schemas. One useful feature is `uniqueConstraints` which lets you define multi-column unique constraints that can't be expressed with just `@Column(unique=true)` — for example, unique combination of first name and last name.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Table is optional until your Java class name and your database table name don't match — then it's essential.

beats.heading: What it does
beats.body: @Table tells JPA which database table this entity maps to. Without it, JPA uses the class name. A User class maps to a user table. An OrderItem class maps to an orderitem table. When your actual table name is different — like tbl_users or order_item — you need @Table(name="...") to specify it.

beats.heading: What you can configure
items: name — the table name. The most commonly used attribute.
schema — specify the database schema. Useful in PostgreSQL where tables are in named schemas.
uniqueConstraints — define multi-column unique constraints that a single @Column(unique=true) can't express.

beats.heading: Multi-column unique constraints
beats.body: @Column(unique=true) constrains a single column. When you need a combination to be unique — like first name plus last name — you need @Table(uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = {"first_name", "last_name"})). This constraint goes on the table, not on an individual column.

beats.heading: Gotcha
beats.body: gotcha: Spring Boot applies a naming strategy that converts camelCase field names to snake_case column names automatically. So firstName becomes first_name in the database without any @Column annotation. The same strategy may affect your table name. If your entity is UserProfile, Spring Boot maps it to user_profile. Be explicit with @Table if your actual table name is different.

sections.cap: Use @Table when your database table name differs from the class name, when you need schema qualification, or when you need a multi-column unique constraint.
followup_handoff: Spring Boot's naming strategy is a common follow-up — it explains why camelCase fields become snake_case columns.
They might ask how to create a composite unique key — @Table uniqueConstraints is the JPA way.

followup_questions: What is the default table name for a @Entity class in Spring Boot?
How does Spring Boot's naming strategy affect entity-to-table mapping?
How do you create a multi-column unique constraint in JPA?

question: What is @Temporal in JPA and how do you map dates?
title: @Temporal and Date Mapping in JPA
direct_answer: In JPA (pre-Java 8), **`@Temporal`** specified how `java.util.Date` or `java.util.Calendar` mapped to the database: `TemporalType.DATE` (date only), `TIMESTAMP` (date+time), `TIME` (time only). For Java 8+, use `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` directly — no `@Temporal` needed.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Still using @Temporal with Java 8+ date types — it's not needed for java.time

sections.title: Date Mapping: Legacy vs Modern
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Temporal` is only needed for `java.util.Date`/`Calendar` (legacy)
- Java 8 `java.time` types map directly — no `@Temporal`
- `LocalDate` → SQL `DATE`, `LocalDateTime` → SQL `TIMESTAMP`
- `Instant` → `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`
- `@CreationTimestamp` (Hibernate) auto-sets on insert
- `@UpdateTimestamp` (Hibernate) auto-sets on update
- Always prefer `java.time` for new code

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Temporal` was needed in older JPA code when using `java.util.Date` to specify whether to map as a DATE, TIMESTAMP, or TIME column. With Java 8 and the `java.time` API, this is no longer needed — `LocalDate` maps to a DATE column, `LocalDateTime` maps to TIMESTAMP automatically, and JPA handles the conversion. I always recommend using the Java 8 date API for new code. Hibernate also provides `@CreationTimestamp` and `@UpdateTimestamp` annotations which automatically set the field to the current timestamp on insert and update respectively, which is very convenient for audit fields.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Temporal is a legacy annotation. If you're using Java 8 date types, you don't need it at all.

beats.heading: What @Temporal was for
beats.body: Before Java 8, Java had java.util.Date, which holds both date and time. @Temporal told JPA which part to store — TemporalType.DATE for date only, TIMESTAMP for date plus time, or TIME for time only. Without it, JPA didn't know which database column type to use.

beats.heading: The modern approach
beats.body: Java 8 introduced the java.time package with dedicated types for each case. JPA supports them natively — no @Temporal needed. LocalDate maps to a DATE column. LocalDateTime maps to TIMESTAMP. LocalTime maps to TIME. The types are self-describing, so JPA knows exactly what to do.

beats.heading: Hibernate audit helpers
items: @CreationTimestamp — Hibernate automatically sets this LocalDateTime field to the current time when the entity is first inserted.
@UpdateTimestamp — Hibernate automatically updates this field to the current time on every UPDATE.

beats.heading: Non-obvious
beats.body: non-obvious: if you see @Temporal in existing code, it's probably a legacy codebase using java.util.Date. You can migrate to LocalDateTime incrementally — just swap the field type, remove @Temporal, and the mapping still works. The database column type stays the same.

sections.cap: Use LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and LocalTime for all new code. They map to DATE, TIMESTAMP, and TIME automatically. @Temporal is legacy — you'll encounter it in old code but shouldn't write it in new code.
followup_handoff: They might ask why java.time is preferred over java.util.Date — immutability and timezone handling are the main reasons.
@CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp are useful follow-ups for audit column patterns.

followup_questions: How does LocalDateTime map to a database column?
Why is java.time preferred over java.util.Date?

question: What is @Transient in JPA?
title: @Transient Annotation in JPA
direct_answer: **`@Transient`** marks a field that should NOT be persisted to the database. JPA ignores `@Transient` fields when reading from and writing to the database. Use it for calculated fields, temporary state, or fields you want in the Java class but not in the table.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between @Transient and Java's transient keyword

sections.title: @Transient Usage
Key Points
sections.content:
- `@Transient` → field excluded from JPA persistence (no DB column)
- Java `transient` keyword → field excluded from Java serialization (different!)
- Use for: calculated values, temporary state, cached data
- Works with `@PostLoad` to compute value after loading entity
- Does NOT affect JSON serialization — field still appears in JSON
- Use `@JsonIgnore` if you also want to exclude from JSON response

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: `@Transient` tells JPA to ignore a field — don't include it in any SQL INSERT, UPDATE, or SELECT statements, and don't expect a corresponding column in the database. It's useful for computed or derived fields that you want in the Java class for convenience but don't need to store. For example, an order's total might be computed from subtotal plus tax. The most common gotcha is confusing `@Transient` with Java's `transient` keyword — Java's transient is for serialization (like when you serialize an object to a byte stream), while JPA's `@Transient` is specifically about database persistence. They do different things and you might need both on the same field in some cases.

sections.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with Hibernate and PostgreSQL
sections.hook: @Transient is the opt-out annotation — it tells JPA to ignore a field completely when talking to the database.

beats.heading: What it does
beats.body: JPA maps every non-static, non-transient field in an entity class to a database column by default. @Transient tells JPA to skip a specific field — don't include it in INSERT, UPDATE, or SELECT statements, and don't expect a matching column in the table.

beats.heading: When to use it
beats.body: The most common case is computed fields. If your Order entity stores subtotal and tax in the database, you might want a total field that adds them up. You don't need to store total — it's derived. Mark it @Transient and compute it in a @PostLoad method so it's ready after every database load.

beats.heading: Sharp edge
beats.body: sharp edge: @Transient (JPA annotation) and the Java transient keyword are different things that do different jobs. The Java transient keyword tells the Java serialization mechanism to skip a field. JPA's @Transient tells JPA to skip a field. A field can be transient for serialization but still persisted by JPA, or vice versa. They're completely independent.

beats.heading: What @Transient does NOT do
items: It does not exclude the field from JSON responses — use @JsonIgnore for that.
It does not prevent the field from being set or read in Java — it's a normal field at the Java level.

sections.cap: @Transient = JPA skips this field. Java transient = serialization skips this field. They're separate concerns. Use @Transient for computed or cached values you don't want stored in the database.
followup_handoff: They might follow up with @PostLoad — the JPA lifecycle callback that runs after an entity is loaded.
The @JsonIgnore distinction is a common follow-up for candidates who mention REST APIs.
